# Code Quality

Write the simplest correct code. Preserve semantic accuracy, separation of concerns, clear layers, and maintainability.

## Load the language reference

Read the reference for each language, stack, or domain the change touches before writing or reviewing it. This file owns the language-neutral rules; a reference owns its subject's decisions.

| Language or stack | Reference |
| --- | --- |
| Go | [references/go.md](references/go.md) |
| TypeScript, JavaScript, TSX | [references/typescript.md](references/typescript.md) |
| Python | [references/python.md](references/python.md) |
| Bash, POSIX shell | [references/shell.md](references/shell.md) |
| Local Make targets, pnpm scripts, or CI checks | [references/workflow.md](references/workflow.md) |
| Kotlin, coroutines, kotlinx libraries | [references/kotlin.md](references/kotlin.md) |
| User-facing flows, controls, feedback, and layout | [ux-ui-design](../ux-ui-design/SKILL.md) |
| Android: Compose UI, manifests, resources, launcher icons, instrumented tests | [android-code-quality](../android-code-quality/SKILL.md) |
| Browser UI: components, styling, accessibility, motion, bundles | [web-frontend-quality](../web-frontend-quality/SKILL.md) |
| Data visualization: charts, dashboards, dense analytical displays | [data-visualization](../data-visualization/SKILL.md) |
| Serialized fields, on-disk formats, caches, logs, or a data migration | [references/persistence.md](references/persistence.md) |

Rust, C++, SQL, markup, and unlisted languages follow this file. A repository that pins a language version or toolchain overrides an assumption stated in a reference.

## Design boundaries and APIs

- Treat compatibility and code churn as constraints only when the user, repository, or external consumers require them. Ask when uncertainty would change the design. When you propose less than the user's stated goal, say what remains unmet and why; churn alone does not justify a partial goal.
- When factoring a function, prefer the best coherent signature and update its call sites. Do not retain obsolete parameters or weaker abstractions solely to avoid local churn.
- Choose production APIs and ownership from production needs, not test convenience. Reject parameters, wrappers, interfaces, options, and exposed state whose only justification is easier tests. Inject dependencies only at boundaries that production needs independently of tests. When the better production design makes tests harder, adapt the tests, including integration or subprocess tests; do not retain a worse design to keep unit tests simple.
- Prefer direct commands and existing tool defaults. Add wrappers, configuration, custom bookkeeping, or orchestration only for a demonstrated gap in current production requirements.
- When a feature becomes unused or is replaced, remove the whole feature: implementation, configuration settings and defaults, validation, fallbacks, tests for the deleted behavior, and documentation. Keep compatibility only for a concrete consumer requirement; hypothetical older deployments do not justify retaining an obsolete feature. A parameter, field, or result whose only possible value is one value everywhere is dead, as is a symbol reachable only from tests unless the repository documents it as a test seam. Before deleting an exported symbol, prove unreachability for every consumer: sibling repositories, interface implementations, reflection and JSON entry points, generated bindings, and documented API.
- Establish invariants once at the owning boundary. A fallback or accessor that tolerates a state the constructor cannot produce hides a path that bypasses the invariant: make construction own the state or delete the tolerance.
- Put implementation assumptions and failure modes beside the source code that owns them. Use broader documentation only for concepts or workflows with no natural source-code owner. Reserve `AGENTS.md` for instructions on how to work in the repository, not descriptions of runtime behavior. Link to the owning source instead of duplicating it. When removing or replacing behavior, delete documentation of the old mechanism and backward-compatibility notes. Document only the current contract and user actions. Never describe legacy behavior or past implementation choices in current documentation or code comments; historical facts belong in Git history.
- Mark incomplete implementations and placeholders with a `TODO` beside the owning code. State the missing behavior and concrete follow-up so later work is discoverable. A TODO does not justify presenting incomplete behavior as implemented or leaving authorized work unfinished.
- Use `TODO(YYYY-MM-DD)` for deprecation or cleanup deferred to a later time. State what must change and the condition for removal or reconsideration.
- Do not repeat defensive checks in methods when construction or encapsulation guarantees them. Validate each input once at the boundary that owns it. Add a second check only when it guards a different trust level, such as a file the user edits versus state the tool wrote.
- Keep one source of truth. Before adding a field, check whether its value can be derived cheaply from existing state. Store it only when it represents an independent choice or measured performance requires caching. Read owned data from its owner instead of copying values that must stay equal. Put each responsibility in one layer; a second owner for state, validation, or behavior is a defect.
- Name symbols and control flow for the real semantics. A misleading name is a defect, not a style preference.
- Never hand-edit a generated artifact. Change the generator, regenerate, and exclude its output from formatting, lint, and review through the repository's ignore mechanism.
- Surface errors. Never hide failure or rely on a fragile fallback. A failure must not leave partial state, write stale data, or report false success.

## Preserve security, contracts, and failure paths

- Validate untrusted input at the boundary that owns it, and fail closed. A parse, authentication, authorization, or validation error never falls through to success.
- Enforce authentication and authorization at one point. Do not add a weaker second path.
- Keep secrets, tokens, and raw credentials out of logs, errors, and committed files.
- Parameterize queries and escape output. Never build an executable string, command, or query from untrusted input.
- Keep API, schema, routing, identity, and provenance contracts explicit and preserved. Serialized, cached, logged, and wire fields follow [references/persistence.md](references/persistence.md).
- Handle normal, edge, concurrent, retry, and failure paths. Make a retry idempotent or guarded by request identity.

## Optimize application performance

- Do not add material waste in I/O, queries, allocation, payload, CPU, or latency.
- For files, network bodies, logs, and other input whose size can grow, use chunked readers or iterators with bounded working memory and backpressure. Do not materialize the whole input merely to forward it or inspect a prefix. Whole-input reads require an explicit small size bound and a consumer that needs the complete value. Propagate cancellation and errors, and release resources when the consumer stops early.
- Add a benchmark only to investigate a plausible, material effect on application-level latency, throughput, memory use, or capacity under a realistic workload. Before benchmarking an isolated component, establish how its cost and execution frequency contribute to that effect. A large percentage improvement in a negligible component does not justify a benchmark. Without that application-level connection, do not add one unless explicitly requested.

## Test behavior

- Investigate slow tests and test suites before accepting their runtime. Measure uncached per-test timings, identify the dominant waits or work, and fix avoidable cost without weakening coverage. Use virtual time or explicit synchronization instead of real sleeps for expiry, polling, retries, and asynchronous ordering. Parallelism, caching, longer timeouts, or a passing result do not resolve an unexplained slowdown; report before/after timings and explain any essential remaining cost.
- Every test must have a concrete purpose: exercise a specific edge case or regression, or increase coverage of reachable behavior. For a small defaulting change, first inspect existing behavioral coverage. Add fixtures, servers, or helpers only when an uncovered regression or contract justifies their maintenance cost. Remove tests that only restate implementation logic without either benefit.
- Reproduce a bug with a test before fixing it. Choose the correct fix, not the quickest patch.
- When removing functionality, do not add a test whose only purpose is to confirm its absence. Remove or update tests for the deleted behavior.
- Do not worry about code churn in tests. Freely restructure, rename, or rewrite tests to follow these rules; a large test diff is not a reason to preserve a weaker structure.
- Do not write mirror tests that copy, import, or recompute a production constant, template, query, or algorithm as the expected value. They cannot fail independently of the implementation and, when copied, create a second source of truth. Assert the smallest observable contract or invariant instead. An exact full-value assertion is appropriate only when the literal itself is an external compatibility contract, fixture, or approved golden output.
- Test observable behavior. Build values through their owning constructor rather than a literal that skips an invariant.

## Keep mechanical conventions

- When a linter exception is justified, suppress the specific rule inline at the narrowest supported scope and explain why. Change project linter configuration only when explicitly requested.
- In languages that support both forms, use `//` line comments instead of `/* */` blocks.
- Keep `.gitignore` sorted.
- Sort enum values and lists of strings by default unless their order has semantic meaning.

## Shape useful Git history

- Stop dependent Git operations when a mutation fails; do not mask its exit status with a later inspection command. Before amending, confirm HEAD is the expected task-owned commit and inspect the staged diff. A failed commit must not lead to amending the previous commit.
- Use a concise subject no longer than 120 characters and wrap body lines at 80 columns. Default to a body; omit it only for an obviously trivial, self-explanatory change such as a typo, formatting-only change, or comment-only change. Changes that affect behavior, interfaces, dependencies, data, architecture, or multiple meaningful concerns require a body. Explain the rationale and consequential tradeoffs with detail proportional to the change; do not restate the subject or diff. Use the final user handoff as a completeness check: material facts worth reporting there, such as the root cause, behavioral fix, important limitations or tradeoffs, and validation, usually belong in the squashed commit body too. Exclude transient execution chatter and details that do not help a future maintainer. Record change history in commits, never in a Markdown file that lists your changes.
- After completing a code change and its verification, create a cohesive commit before ending the turn, unless the user explicitly asks not to commit or the work is incomplete or blocked. Unless the user requests separate commits, consolidate the current task's commits that exist only above the tracked upstream tip into one cohesive commit before handoff. Verify the upstream and refs before treating commits as unshared; do not fold unrelated work together or rewrite commits that may already be shared.
- Rebase onto the tracked upstream branch as needed to incorporate its changes before continuing or handing off work.

## Verify and control scope

- Do not leave build, lint, or test failures caused by the change unresolved. Report pre-existing failures and quality violations; ask before widening scope to fix unrelated ones. Honor explicit repository gates, including applicable conditional suites, tags, and platforms. Otherwise select the smallest checks that prove the affected behavior. After a small follow-up fix, rerun affected checks and retain passing evidence for unchanged paths; repeat broad suites only when required or when the change invalidates their evidence. Missing evidence for an affected path remains a validation gap.
- For background verification, track the exact worker or run identity and let its owning process persist the exit code. Poll that result before reporting success; process disappearance proves only termination. Confirm expected artifacts and publication separately. Report the stage that passed or failed, not an inferred overall result.
- For mechanical rewrites, keep substitutions line-scoped; never let a match cross a statement. Inspect the diff for lost punctuation, arguments, or changed meaning at unintended sites. When equivalence is clear by inspection, retain the existing validation evidence; uncertainty requires checks for the affected behavior.
- Assume memory is stale. Prefer current primary documentation and upstream source repositories; clone documentation repositories when practical. Repository instructions and the language references own technology-specific sources.
